title: What a Coursebook Is and What It Is Not
brief: Define a coursebook as a published, sequenced teaching resource that provides syllabus structure, language input, and practice activities across a level or course. Distinguish it from supplementary materials, workbooks, and teacher's resource packs. Explain the central tension: a coursebook is a tool, not a curriculum authority — the teacher remains the professional decision-maker. Use a brief hypothetical to illustrate what happens when a teacher follows a book page-by-page without thought (e.g., a unit on 'booking a hotel' delivered to a class of ten-year-olds who have never travelled alone).

title: Evaluating a Coursebook Before You Adopt It
brief: Walk through a practical checklist a teacher can apply when assessing whether a coursebook suits their context. Cover five key criteria: (1) level and progression — does the language grading match the learners? (2) topic and cultural relevance — are the themes appropriate and engaging for this age group and culture? (3) skills balance — does the book give adequate attention to all four skills? (4) grammar and vocabulary coverage — is the syllabus explicit and logical? (5) layout and usability — are instructions clear and activities easy to set up? Stress that no book will score perfectly on every criterion, and the evaluation goal is to identify gaps before teaching begins, not to find a perfect product. Invent a short hypothetical scenario of a teacher comparing two books for an adult beginner class.

title: Using a Coursebook Flexibly: The Teacher as Editor
brief: Explain the concept of 'principled use': following the book's overall structure while making deliberate, reasoned choices about sequence, pace, and emphasis. Describe three common flexible-use strategies — reordering activities within a lesson to suit a warmer-to-cooler energy arc, splitting a dense double-page spread across two lessons, and combining two short units that share a grammar point. Emphasise that flexibility should be driven by learner needs and lesson aims, not by personal preference or time pressure alone. Use a hypothetical example of a teacher who notices that the coursebook introduces the present perfect before students have consolidated simple past, and decides to delay the new unit by one week.

title: Adapting Coursebook Activities
brief: Cover the four main adaptation techniques: adding (extending an activity with extra practice), removing (cutting a task that is too easy, too difficult, or culturally inappropriate), modifying (changing the format, grouping, or focus of an existing task), and replacing (substituting a coursebook exercise with a teacher-made equivalent that meets the same aim). For each technique, provide a short hypothetical classroom example — for instance, modifying a written gap-fill into a spoken information-gap activity, or replacing a reading text about a cultural event unfamiliar to the class with a parallel text the teacher writes on a locally familiar topic. Remind writers that adaptation should preserve the original lesson aim even when the activity changes significantly.

title: Supplementing and Skipping: Knowing When the Book Is Not Enough
brief: Distinguish supplementing (adding material the book does not cover) from skipping (omitting material that is unnecessary or unsuitable). Explain legitimate reasons to supplement: a grammar point the book treats too briefly, a skills gap (e.g., the book has no extended listening practice at this level), or a motivational need (e.g., a topical news story that connects to the unit theme). Explain legitimate reasons to skip: a topic already mastered by the class, a culturally sensitive subject, or a task type that duplicates one done recently. Caution against skipping simply because a section looks difficult to teach — that is a prompt to prepare more carefully, not to omit. Invent a brief example of a teacher supplementing a unit on giving directions with a short teacher-created audio dialogue.

title: Building a Healthy Long-Term Relationship with Your Coursebook
brief: Synthesise the unit by framing the coursebook as a professional partnership rather than an authority or an obstacle. Encourage teachers to annotate their books after each lesson — noting what worked, what fell flat, and what they changed — so that adaptation becomes faster and more confident over time. Introduce the habit of 'pre-reading' the next two or three units before teaching the current one, so that decisions about skipping or reordering are made with full awareness of what is coming. Close by reinforcing that a well-used coursebook frees the teacher to focus on interaction and responsiveness in the classroom, because the structural planning work has already been done.
